    PDT – Formal Definition A Pushdown Transducer A PDT is a tuple ⟨Q, I, Γ, δ, q0, Z0, F, O, η⟩ where * Q is a finite set of states. * I is a finite input alphabet. * Γ is a finite stack alphabet. * δ, the transition function, is a partial function from Q × (I ∪ {ϵ}) × Γ to the set of finite subsets of Q × Γ. q0 ∈ Q, the initial state. * Z0 ∈ Γ, the initial stack symbol. * F ⊆ Q, the set of accepting states. * O is the output alphabet * η : Q × (I ∪ {ϵ}) × Γ → O*, translation function 8 / 35

    Pushdown Transducer Example 1 L = {aⁿbⁿ | n > 0}, τ(aⁿbⁿ) = bⁿ.

      • q1 has a self-loop labeled b, A/ϵ, b.
      • Transition from q1 to qF (accepting state) labeled ϵ, Z0/Z0, ϵ.

    Operations on FSA Suppose L₁ and L₂ are both regular languages. Then * L₁ ∪ L₂ is also regular, * L₁ ∩ L₂ is also regular, * L₁  L₂ is also regular, * L₁ᶜ is also regular. 12 / 35

    Slide 13

    Operations on FSA Definition We say that the class of languages C is closed under an operation O, if, for any languages L₁, . . . , Lₙ ∈ C, we have O(L₁, . . . , Lₙ) ∈ C.

    Examples C(L) = Lᶜ ∪(L₁, L₂) = L₁ ∪ L₂ 13 / 35

    Slide 14

    Operations on FSA Let FSA be the class of regular (recognized by a FSA) languages. If L₁, L₂ ∈ FSA, then * L₁ ∪ L₂ ∈ FSA, * L₁ ∩ L₂ ∈ FSA, * L₁  L₂ ∈ FSA, * L₁ᶜ ∈ FSA.

    Fact FSA is closed under ∪, ∩, , ᶜ 14 / 35

    Slide 15

    Operations on FSA

    ∪ ∩ \ ᶜ
    FSA yes yes yes yes
    DPDA
    • yes means the class of languages is closed under an operation
    • no means the class of languages is not closed under an operation 15 / 35

    Pumping Lemma for PDA Bar-Hillel lemma If L ⊆ Σ* is a recognized by a NPDA language then there exists m ⩾ 1 such that any w ∈ L with |w| ⩾ m can be represented as w = x₁x₂x₃x₄x₅ such that * |x₂x₄| > 0, * |x₂x₃x₄| ⩽ m, * x₁x₂ⁱx₃x₄ⁱx₅ ∈ L for any i ⩾ 1.

    Example L = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n > 0} is not recognized by any DPDA (moreover, is not recognized by any NPDA). 24 / 35

ℕ⁺ is the set of positive natural numbers. ▶ L₃ = {xcy | x, y ∈ {a, b}* ∧ |x| > 0 ∧ |y| > 0 ∧ |x| = |y| ∧ y ≠ xᴿ} (where xᴿ is the reversed string x), the alphabet is I = {a, b, c}, and translates it into y ▶ L₄ = {aⁿbᵐ | m, n ∈ ℕ and n ≤ m ≤ 2n}, and translates it into aⁿbⁿ 6 / 7

    Slide 6

    Recap questions for midterm topics * There are languages that are not regular. What does it mean? * Do you remember some of the consequences of Pumping Lemma? * Do you remember the difference between bounded and unbounded memory? * What are the acceptance criteria for a PDA? 6

    Slide 7

    Fixed vs finite memory (1) * Regular languages are languages which can be recognized by an automaton with fixed memory * Fixed memory (bounded) is more restrictive than infinite (unbounded)! * Finite (bounded) vs. unlimited (unbounded) * Think about FSA (states only) and PDA (stack can grow) * FSA is a model of computation with fixed memory * PDA has finite but not fixed * It is using an unbounded amount of memory 7

    Slide 8

    Fixed vs finite memory (2) * Many languages cannot be recognized using only fixed memory * For example aⁿbⁿ * FSA cannot count an unlimited n * Number of states is fixed, stack can grow with no bound 8

    Slide 9

    PDA and compilers * PDA are at the heart of compilers * Stack memory has a LIFO policy * LIFO is suitable to analyze nested syntactic structures * Arithmetical expressions * Begin/End * Activation records * Parenthesized strings * … 9

    Slide 10

    What are context-free languages? 10

    PD transducer, formally A PD transducer (PDT) is a tuple <Q, I, Γ, δ, q0, Z0, F, O, η> * Q is a finite set of states * … * F ⊆ Q is the set of final states * O is the output alphabet * η: Q×(I∪{ϵ})×Γ→O*

    Remarks * Q, I, Γ, δ, q0, Z0 and F are defined as in “acceptor” PDA * η is defined only where δ is defined * The stack can be necessary for two reasons: * The language to be recognized requires it * The translation requires it 22

    Slide 23

    Configuration A configuration c is <q, x, γ, z> * q∈Q is the current state of the control device * x∈I* is the unread portion of the input string * γ∈Γ* is the string of symbols in the stack * z is the string already written on the output tape 23

    Slide 24

    Transitions, formally * If δ(q, i, A) = <q’,α> is defined and η(q, i, A)=w then * c=<q, iy, Aγ, z> |– c’=<q’, y, αγ, zw> * If δ(q, ϵ, A) = <q’,α> is defined and η(q, ϵ, A)=w then * c=<q, x, Aγ, z> |– c’=<q’, x, αγ, zw>

    Theoretical Computer Science Operations on PDA Lecture 7 - Manuel Mazzara 27

    Slide 28

    Closure properties * Closure properties of languages accepted by deterministic PDA (by final state) are different than those of languages accepted by nondeterministic PDA * We will see this later with related implications * Deterministic PDA are closed under complementation * The class of deterministic context-free languages is closed under complement * The class of non-deterministic context free languages is not closed under complement * Deterministic PDA are NOT closed under union 28

    Slide 29

    PDA and complement * The class of languages recognized by deterministic PDAs is closed under complement * The complement can be algorithmically built by: * Eliminating loops (Blue arrow points here: “Avoid infinite computations!”) * Completing δ * Swapping final and non-final states (Blue arrow points here: “Same than FSA!”) 29

    Slide 30

    Why the swap itself does not work? * To find the complement of a PDA we could flip final and non-final states as we did for FSA. This does not work! * The PDA P with input, for example, x could lead to a state q which is not a final state but, performing an ϵ-move, could reach accepting state q′ * Let us flip states and obtain P’, which also ends in q after processing the input x. q is a final state now so P’ will also accept x * Both PDA and PDA’ accept x, so we did not build the complement 30

    Slide 31

    Acyclic PDA (preliminary definitions) * In order to overcome this problem, we must make sure that no ϵ-moves can happen after we read the last input symbol * Given a PDA we define: <q,x,α>|- * -d <q’,y,β> * |- * -d is a sequence of moves that needs a symbol to proceed * Remember the ϵ-move! * <q,x,α>|- * -<q’,y,β> and for β=Zβ’ δ(q’,ϵ,Z)=⊥ (undefined) * You cannot proceed without consuming an input symbol * ϵ-move is not available 31

    Slide 32

    Acyclic PDA * A PDA is acyclic if and only if: * ∀x∈I* <q0,x,Z0>|- * -d<q,ϵ,γ> for some q and γ * it always reads the whole input string and then stops * It does not loop after having consumed all the input * Every deterministic PDA can be transformed into an equivalent acyclic PDA * Adding the acyclic condition does not reduce the power * The proof is a bit tricky, the idea is to do loops elimination * We will not show the proof here 32

    Slide 33

    PDA and complement * The class of languages recognized by deterministic PDAs is closed under complement * The complement can be algorithmically built by: * Eliminating loops (Blue arrow points here: “Avoid infinite computations!”) * Completing δ * Swapping final and non-final states (Blue arrow points here: “Same than FSA!”) 33

    Slide 34

    Loops elimination * Loops elimination is essential, otherwise the end of the computation may never be reached * What if there are sequences of ϵ-moves traversing some final and some non-final states (and the input is entirely read)? * With these precautions, we are sure that either the PDA or its complement will accept the string 34

    Slide 35

    Union * The class of languages recognized by PDA is not closed under union * There is no PDA that recognizes {aⁿbⁿ|n≥1}∪{aⁿb²ⁿ|n≥1}, but * {aⁿbⁿ|n≥1} is recognizable by PDA (Blue arrow points here: “We have seen this”) * {aⁿb²ⁿ|n≥1} is recognizable by PDA (Blue arrow points here: “Straightforward consequence”) * Idea: after a sequence of a’s, it is not possible to deterministically decide whether start processing single b’s or pairs of b’s * A nondeterministic PDA can do instead 35

    Slide 36

    Not a deterministic context-free language! L={aⁿbⁿ|n ≥ 1} ∪ {aⁿb²ⁿ|n ≥ 1} is a CFL and not a DCFL

    • We can design a nondeterministic PDA that recognize L
    • We cannot design a deterministic PDA that recognize L
    • It is easy to construct a NPDA for {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}
    • And for {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 1}
    • These two can be joined by a new start state and epsilon-transitions to create a NPDA for L 36

    Slide 37

    Why? * The stack has to be prepared in the push phase to be ready to manage the pop phase * If not prepared accordingly we are not able to manage the second part of the input string * A nondeterministic version would just manage the two possibilities in parallel 37

    Slide 38

    Nondeterminism and proof sketch

    • Image description: Two diagrams illustrating Nondeterminism.
      • Left diagram: Shows a split. A state labeled aⁿ PUSH transitions to two possible states: bⁿ POP via b, and b²ⁿ POP via b. Text {aⁿbⁿ|n≥1} and {aⁿb²ⁿ|n≥1} are next to the pop states.
      • Right diagram: Shows a combined state. State aⁿ PUSH transitions via b to a state bⁿ OR b²ⁿ POP. 38

    Slide 39

    Intuitive proof sketch * There is an initial push-phase in which a’s are read from input and pushed on the stack, then there is a pop-phase * After n pops of a’s and scanning b’s from input, the stack is emptied and the input has not been fully scanned: * There are more b’s than a’s in the input string * THE STRING DOES NOT BELONG TO aⁿ bⁿ * It may be still aⁿb²ⁿ but the content of the stack is now lost * n is forgotten – we cannot count anymore! * Could be b³ⁿ or anything else * The stack is not emptied after popping a’s and scanning all the b’s from input: * There are not less a’s than b’s * You previously pushed 2 a’s on stack for each a’s in input to recognize aⁿb²ⁿ but the string in input does not have this shape * It may be aⁿ bⁿ then but… * If there are no more b’s in input to scan, it is impossible to know whether the stack contains exactly n symbols

    • Image description: A diagram showing state aⁿ PUSH branching via b to a state bⁿ OR b²ⁿ POP contained within a larger bounding box, indicating the non-deterministic state collapse/merger described in the text. 39

    Slide 40

    Another example of non-closure L₁ = {aⁱbʲcᵏ, i, j, k ≥ 0 and i ≠ j} (recognizable by PDA) L₂ = {aⁱbʲcᵏ, i, j, k ≥ 0 and j ≠ k} (recognizable by PDA)

    L₃ = L₁ ∪ L₂ = {aⁱbʲcᵏ, i, j, k ≥ 0 and ((i ≠ j) or (j ≠ k))}

    Is L₃ recognizable by PDA? 40

    Slide 41

    Intersection and difference * The class of languages recognized by PDAs is not closed under intersection * A∪B=(Aᶜ∩Bᶜ)ᶜ * Since PDA languages are closed under complement, if they were closed under intersection, they should be closed under union as well * The class of languages recognized by PDAs is not closed under difference * A-B = A ∩ Bᶜ * Since PDA languages are closed under complement, if they were closed under difference, they should be closed under intersection and union as well 41

    Slide 42

    Recap * We have seen that the union of some languages recognized by PDAs cannot be recognized by any PDA * PDAs are not closed under union * Example: * L₁={aⁿbⁿ|n≥1} * L₂={aⁿb²ⁿ|n≥1} * … but L₁∪L₂ is not recognizable by any PDA 42

    Slide 43

    Closure of operations

    Operations Regular Context-free Deterministic CF
    union yes yes no
    intersection yes no no
    complement yes no yes
